plan.topic: Retatrutide vs semaglutide 2 mg in type 2 diabetes: TRANSCEND-T2D-2, the first randomized Phase 3 head-to-head (Lilly topline, Oct 28, 2026), explained alongside the peer-reviewed retatrutide evidence
plan.angle:
Lane C (log 'lane: C'), 8–12 min, 14:00 ET. First sentence answers the title with a 'you' scenario: 'You have type 2 diabetes and you're on semaglutide. In the first head-to-head trial, retatrutide lowered A1C and weight more, but more people stopped it because of side effects.' News figures, all credited 'Lilly, Oct 28, 2026; company-reported, not yet peer-reviewed; open-label; if everyone stayed on treatment':
- 1,298 adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin, with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor; baseline A1C 7.0–10.5%; 80 weeks; 2:2:1 randomization (per-arm n from the release).
- A1C −2.2 points on retatrutide 9 mg and 12 mg vs −1.8 on semaglutide 2 mg. Give mmol/mol only if the release supports it.
- Weight −19.5% / −20.9% vs −9.4%.
- Side effects, each with its semaglutide rate: diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting per arm; stopping because of side effects 4.8% / 7.9% vs 2.7%; dysesthesia 4.8% / 6.5% vs 2.7%.
The body rests on settled evidence:
(1) What is retatrutide? The GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptors explained (peer-reviewed mechanism sources).
(2) What did this trial actually test? Open-label design and what the 'stayed on treatment' measure means. Never say 'estimand'.
(3) How do the results compare with retatrutide's earlier trials? TRIUMPH-2 (Lancet: 1,152 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight, 80 weeks, vs placebo) and TRANSCEND-T2D-1 (Lancet, 40 weeks, vs placebo), each labelled as a separate trial.
(4) Why do people with type 2 diabetes lose less weight on these drugs? Separate trials, not head-to-head.
(5) What is dysesthesia? Say only what's confirmed, and that the cause isn't known.
(6) Is retatrutide approved? Investigational, not approved by the FDA, MHRA, Health Canada or TGA as of Oct 29, 2026. Lilly says it plans to file in Q1 2027, and a plan to file isn't approval.
(7) What does this mean if you're on semaglutide now? Nothing changes today. 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.'
No 'up to 60 pounds' framing and no 'beat' verdict beyond the reported numbers. Never mention online or research-peptide sources; for approved options or a clinical trial, ask a prescriber. Re-hook every 45–75 s. One subscribe ask, after the side-effects payoff. Include 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' Thumbnail: 4 words or fewer, reaction layout with one labelled character (e.g. 'First Real Matchup'), not big-number.

package.description:
In Lilly's company-reported, not-yet-peer-reviewed trial in type 2 diabetes, retatrutide lowered A1C and weight more than semaglutide 2 mg, but more people stopped for side effects, and dysesthesia (abnormal skin sensations) was more common.

Not personal advice. Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

TRANSCEND-T2D-2: 80 weeks, 1,298 adults on metformin, open-label, reported as if everyone stayed on treatment. A1C fell 2.2 points on retatrutide 9 mg and 12 mg vs 1.8 on semaglutide 2 mg; weight fell 19.5% and 20.9% vs 9.4%. Stopped for side effects: 4.8% and 7.9% vs 2.7%. Retatrutide is investigational and not approved anywhere.

Sources:
1. Eli Lilly press release, Oct 28, 2026 (via BioSpace): https://www.biospace.com/press-releases/lillys-retatrutide-delivered-greater-a1c-reduction-and-more-than-double-the-weight-loss-of-ozempics-highest-approved-dose-in-head-to-head-trial
2. TRANSCEND-T2D-2, ClinicalTrials.gov: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06260722

script.working_title: Retatrutide vs Semaglutide: First Head-to-Head Results
script.hook_pattern: Visceral 'you' scenario with a direct answer to the title in the first sentence, then an open loop (the unfamiliar side effect, dysesthesia) that pays off late. lane: C

scenes.narration: You have type two diabetes, and you're on semaglutide. In the first head-to-head trial against semaglutide, reh-tuh-TROO-tide lowered A-one-C and weight more than semaglutide, but more people stopped it because of side effects.

visual.stock_query: curious woman reading phone headline on couch

scenes.retention_device: Direct answer to the title in the first sentence (search viewers get the payoff instantly)

scenes.narration: That's the short answer. These results come from Eli Lilly, released on October twenty-eighth, twenty twenty-six. They're company-reported and not yet peer-reviewed, so treat them as a first look.
scenes.retention_device: Credibility frame that sets up what to watch for

scenes.narration: Now imagine Dana. She's fifty-eight, and after months of work, her A-one-C has finally come down on semaglutide. Then a headline lands on her phone: a new drug, about twice the weight loss.

visual.stock_query: woman at kitchen table phone buzzing

scenes.narration: Her first feeling isn't excitement. It's a knot in her stomach. Am I on the wrong medicine? Did I miss something?
scenes.on_screen_text: Am I on the wrong one?

visual.stock_query: worried woman thought bubble question marks

scenes.narration: If you've felt that, you're not alone. In the next few minutes: the real numbers, what this trial could and couldn't show, and what to ask your prescriber.
scenes.retention_device: Promise of what the viewer gets

scenes.narration: And stay for one side effect on the list that most people have never heard of. It's called dis-es-THEE-zhuh. By the end, you'll know what's confirmed about it, and what nobody knows yet.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop (dysesthesia), paid off in the 'What is dysesthesia?' chapter

scenes.narration: First, what actually is reh-tuh-TROO-tide? Start with what you may already know. Semaglutide acts on one hormone receptor, GLP-one. Tirzepatide acts on two: GLP-one and G-I-P.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change answering a searched question

scenes.narration: Reh-tuh-TROO-tide is designed to act on three: GLP-one, G-I-P, and a third one, glucagon. That's why you'll hear it called a triple agonist.
GLP-one helps the pancreas release insulin when blood sugar rises, and turns down appetite. G-I-P also boosts insulin release after eating.
But here's where it gets weird. Glucagon is the hormone that normally pushes blood sugar up. So why would anyone build it into a diabetes drug?
scenes.retention_device: 'Here's where it gets weird' pattern interrupt

scenes.narration: In the lab research behind reh-tuh-TROO-tide, switching on the glucagon receptor in mice raised how much energy their bodies burned. The GLP-one and G-I-P parts help keep blood sugar in check while that happens.

visual.stock_query: cartoon lab mouse on tiny treadmill

scenes.narration: Think of it as a three-player team: two hold blood sugar steady, one leans on energy use. That's the design. The real test is people, against a medicine that already works well.
That brings us to the new trial, called TRANSCEND T-two-D two. It enrolled one thousand two hundred ninety-eight adults with type two diabetes.
Everyone was already taking metformin, and some were also on an S-G-L-T-two inhibitor, another common diabetes pill. Their starting A-one-C was between seven and ten point five percent.

items: Some also on an SGLT2 inhibitor

scenes.narration: Quick reminder: A-one-C reflects your average blood sugar over roughly the past three months. It's one of the main numbers your diabetes care team tracks.
People were randomly assigned two to two to one: reh-tuh-TROO-tide nine milligrams, reh-tuh-TROO-tide twelve milligrams, or semaglutide two milligrams.
scenes.retention_device: Sets up the three arms viewers will track

scenes.narration: That works out to roughly five hundred twenty people on each reh-tuh-TROO-tide dose, and about two hundred sixty on semaglutide.
And semaglutide two milligrams is a serious opponent. It's the highest dose of semaglutide's weekly diabetes injection, tested against one milligram in the SUSTAIN FORTE trial.
The trial ran for eighty weeks. That's about a year and a half, long enough to see where results settle, not just the early rush.

visual.stock_query: calendar pages flipping season to season

scenes.narration: Now, two details change how you should read every number that follows. Miss them, and the headlines can mislead you.
Detail one: the trial was open-label. People knew which drug they were taking, and so did their doctors. That can nudge how side effects get noticed and reported.

visual.stock_query: clear labelled medicine boxes on table

scenes.narration: Detail two: Lilly reported these results as if everyone stayed on treatment, without adding other diabetes medicines. That estimates what each drug does for people who keep taking it as planned.

visual.stock_query: runners staying on a long path

scenes.narration: Counting everyone who started, including people who stopped, usually gives smaller numbers. Hold on to that, because it comes back in a big way in the side-effects section.

visual.fact: These assume everyone stayed on treatment

scenes.retention_device: Open loop paid off in 'Side effects and stopping'

scenes.narration: So, the results. A-one-C first. Over eighty weeks, on both reh-tuh-TROO-tide doses, nine and twelve milligrams, A-one-C fell by two point two points on average.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change and first big number

scenes.narration: On semaglutide two milligrams, it fell by one point eight points.

To picture that gap: the average starting A-one-C in this trial was eight point three percent. Matching those averages would land near six point one on reh-tuh-TROO-tide, versus six point five on semaglutide.

visual.stock_query: two staircases going down side by side

scenes.narration: Real people rarely match averages exactly. But here's what matters for Dana: both drugs lowered A-one-C a lot. Her semaglutide isn't suddenly failing because something newer showed a bigger drop.
scenes.retention_device: Returns to character thread, relief beat

scenes.narration: Now weight, and this is where the gap opens up. Over eighty weeks, people on reh-tuh-TROO-tide nine milligrams lost nineteen point five percent of their body weight on average.
On reh-tuh-TROO-tide twelve milligrams, twenty point nine percent.
On semaglutide two milligrams, nine point four percent.

Put simply: roughly one-tenth of body weight on semaglutide, versus roughly one-fifth on reh-tuh-TROO-tide, in this trial, for people who stayed on treatment. And weight is one health measure among many.

visual.stock_query: pie chart slices one tenth one fifth

scenes.narration: But here's a puzzle. If you've followed reh-tuh-TROO-tide before, you may remember bigger weight numbers than twenty percent. So why are these smaller? The answer surprises a lot of people.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: new open loop before section change

scenes.section: Why less weight loss with diabetes?
scenes.narration: The drug didn't get weaker. It's a pattern across this whole class of medicines: in trials, people with type two diabetes tend to lose less weight than people without it.
scenes.on_screen_text: Why less weight loss with diabetes?

visual.fact: With type 2 diabetes, weight loss tends to be smaller across this class

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the puzzle, opens the 'why'

scenes.section: Why less weight loss with diabetes?
scenes.narration: Look at semaglutide two point four milligrams. In STEP one, adults without diabetes lost fourteen point nine percent over sixty-eight weeks, versus two point four percent on placebo.

visual.stock_query: bar chart tall bar short bar

scenes.section: Why less weight loss with diabetes?
scenes.narration: In STEP two, adults with type two diabetes on the same dose lost nine point six percent over sixty-eight weeks, versus three point four percent on placebo. Both figures count everyone who started.

scenes.section: Why less weight loss with diabetes?
scenes.narration: Tirzepatide shows the same pattern. On fifteen milligrams over seventy-two weeks, SURMOUNT-one, in adults without diabetes, reported twenty point nine percent, versus three point one on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Pattern repeats with a second drug

scenes.section: Why less weight loss with diabetes?
scenes.narration: SURMOUNT-two, in adults with type two diabetes, reported fourteen point seven percent, versus three point two on placebo. Again, counting everyone who started.

scenes.section: Why less weight loss with diabetes?
scenes.narration: These are separate trials, not head-to-head, with different people. But the direction is the same every time.

scenes.section: Why less weight loss with diabetes?
scenes.narration: Why? Nobody knows for certain. Researchers have suggested reasons such as other diabetes medicines that tend to add weight, like insulin, and less sugar, and its calories, being lost in urine once blood sugar improves.

items: Fewer sugar calories lost in urine

scenes.section: Why less weight loss with diabetes?
scenes.narration: So the fair comparison is always people with diabetes against people with diabetes. That's exactly what this new trial did, and why it's more useful to Dana than any headline from an obesity trial.
scenes.retention_device: Loop payoff tied back to character

scenes.narration: So how does this fit with what's already peer-reviewed? In twenty twenty-three, The Lancet published a Phase two trial of reh-tuh-TROO-tide in two hundred eighty-one adults with type two diabetes.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change: question to the viewer

scenes.narration: It tested several doses against placebo, and against dulaglutide one point five milligrams, an older weekly GLP-one medicine.
scenes.retention_device: Micro-story of a different trial design

scenes.narration: At twenty-four weeks, A-one-C fell by two point zero two points on reh-tuh-TROO-tide twelve milligrams, versus one point four one on dulaglutide, and almost no change on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Surprising consistency with the new number

scenes.narration: By thirty-six weeks, people on twelve milligrams had lost sixteen point nine percent of their body weight, versus three percent on placebo and two percent on dulaglutide.
That's a separate, smaller, shorter trial with a different comparator, so its numbers can't be lined up directly with the new one. But the direction matches.

A separate Phase two trial, in three hundred thirty-eight adults with obesity or overweight and without diabetes, flagged something worth watching: heart rate rose with higher doses, peaked around twenty-four weeks, then came down.

visual.stock_query: calm heart with gentle pulse line

scenes.retention_device: New surprising fact before the payoff section

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the part that matters most in real life: who kept taking it.

Like semaglutide, reh-tuh-TROO-tide's common side effects are mostly in the gut: nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation. In the new trial, Lilly reported nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation in every group, semaglutide included. Most were mild to moderate, and some were actually more common on semaglutide.

visual.stock_query: cartoon stomach with gentle wavy lines

scenes.retention_device: Chapter change, common side effects named

scenes.narration: Now the number I'd circle. Stopping the drug because of side effects: four point eight percent on reh-tuh-TROO-tide nine milligrams.

visual.stat_label: Stopped for side effects, retatrutide 9 mg

scenes.narration: Seven point nine percent on reh-tuh-TROO-tide twelve milligrams. That's roughly one person in thirteen.

visual.stat_label: Stopped for side effects, retatrutide 12 mg
visual.stock_query: thirteen cartoon people one stepping away

scenes.narration: And two point seven percent on semaglutide two milligrams, roughly one in thirty-seven.

visual.stat_label: Stopped for side effects, semaglutide 2 mg

scenes.narration: Here's where that earlier detail comes back. The headline A-one-C and weight numbers describe people as if they stayed on treatment. They don't show what happened to the people who stopped.

visual.stock_query: sticky note reminder returns to fridge

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the 'if everyone stayed on treatment' loop

scenes.narration: And more people stopped on reh-tuh-TROO-tide, especially at twelve milligrams. In everyday life, a medicine only helps while you can keep taking it. Open-label design may also have shaped how symptoms were noticed.
scenes.on_screen_text: Helps only if you can continue

scenes.narration: So the honest summary is: more effect, and more people stopping. Both are real. Which matters more depends on the person, and that's a conversation for you and your prescriber.

visual.stock_query: balance scale benefit and side effects

scenes.retention_device: Summary beat before the main loop payoff

scenes.narration: Now, that side effect most people have never heard of. Dis-es-THEE-zhuh is a medical term for abnormal skin sensations, such as tingling.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop from the opening

scenes.narration: In this trial, it was reported by four point eight percent of people on reh-tuh-TROO-tide nine milligrams, six point five percent on twelve milligrams, and two point seven percent on semaglutide two milligrams.
Notice that last number. It showed up with semaglutide too, just less often. And remember, this was open-label.
Here's what isn't known: the cause. How long it lasts and how bothersome it was should become clearer once the full data are peer-reviewed.
New or unusual skin sensations on any medicine are worth mentioning to your prescriber. No need to panic. It's simply useful information for them.
If plain, numbers-first breakdowns like this help you, subscribe. When the full peer-reviewed paper comes out, we'll go through what it adds.

visual.stock_query: Medi mascot pointing at subscribe bell

scenes.retention_device: Single subscribe ask tied to a specific next benefit, after the side-effects payoff

scenes.narration: So, is reh-tuh-TROO-tide approved? No. As of October twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-six, it's investigational and hasn't been approved anywhere yet. Lilly is aiming to file with the FDA first.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change answering a searched question

scenes.narration: On its August twenty twenty-six earnings call, Lilly said it aims to submit reh-tuh-TROO-tide to the FDA in the first quarter of twenty twenty-seven, mainly for weight-related uses. A plan to file isn't approval.
If you're interested, the routes are approved medicines or a properly run clinical trial, and your prescriber can talk you through both.
Back to Dana, and to you. What does this mean if you're on semaglutide right now? Nothing changes today.

visual.stock_query: Dana calm with cup of tea

scenes.retention_device: Returns to the character, answers her worry

scenes.narration: In this very trial, semaglutide two milligrams lowered A-one-C by one point eight points and weight by nine point four percent, with the fewest people stopping for side effects. That's real progress.
Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Bring your questions to your next appointment instead.
Here are four questions worth bringing. Is my A-one-C where we want it? How am I handling side effects? What would we weigh if new options are approved? And could a clinical trial suit me?

items: How am I handling side effects?
What if new options are approved?
Could a clinical trial suit me?

scenes.narration: Dana closes the headline feeling calmer. She has numbers now, not hype, and a short list for her next appointment.
scenes.retention_device: Emotional resolution of the character thread

scenes.narration: Quick recap. Bigger drops in A-one-C and weight on reh-tuh-TROO-tide. More people stopping for side effects. A side effect still being understood. And no approval yet.
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.

factcheck.summary: All TRANSCEND-T2D-2 numbers match Lilly's Oct 28, 2026 topline (via the BioSpace copy of the release, AJMC and HCPLive): 1,298 adults; metformin with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor; A1C 7.0–10.5%, mean 8.3%; 2:2:1; open-label; 80 weeks; A1C −2.2/−2.2 vs −1.8; weight −19.5/−20.9 vs −9.4%; stopped for side effects 4.8/7.9 vs 2.7%; dysesthesia 4.8/6.5 vs 2.7%; GI events mostly mild to moderate, with constipation and vomiting higher on semaglutide than on at least one retatrutide dose. All results use the measure that assumes everyone stayed on treatment. The Q1 2027 filing target from the Aug 2026 earnings call is confirmed by BioSpace. The Phase 2 trials, the mouse mechanism, and the STEP 1/2, SURMOUNT-1/2 and SUSTAIN FORTE figures are cited correctly. Framing (mouse vs human, separate-trial caveats, company-reported and not peer-reviewed) and the safety lines are good. Three minor fixes only.

issues.claim: In the first head-to-head trial, retatrutide lowered A1C and weight more than semaglutide
issues.problem: Retatrutide's Phase 2 diabetes trial (s42) already had an active comparator, dulaglutide. 'First head-to-head trial' is only true against semaglutide, or as the first Phase 3 against another incretin medicine.
issues.fix: Narration: "You have type two diabetes, and you're on semaglutide. In the first head-to-head trial against semaglutide, reh-tuh-TROO-tide lowered A-one-C and weight more than semaglutide, but more people stopped it because of side effects."

issues.claim: Lilly reported these results as if everyone stayed on treatment
issues.problem: Lilly's measure also assumes nobody started an extra glucose-lowering medicine. Leaving that out slightly overstates how much the A1C result reflects the drug alone.
issues.fix: Narration: "Detail two: Lilly reported these results as if everyone stayed on treatment, without adding other diabetes medicines. That estimates what each drug does for people who keep taking it as planned."

issues.claim: S11 title: 'entry terms include dysesthesia'; s61: not approved by FDA, MHRA, Health Canada or TGA
issues.problem: MeSH D010292 lists dysesthesia as a related concept, not an entry term, so the source title is wrong. Its scope note (spontaneous skin sensations such as tingling) still supports s55. S12 only covers the FDA filing plan. It doesn't confirm status with the MHRA, Health Canada or the TGA (still very likely not approved).
issues.fix: Retitle S11: "Paresthesia (MeSH descriptor D010292; dysesthesia listed as a related concept)". In s61, keep the narration, or change it to "It's investigational and hasn't been approved anywhere yet. Lilly is aiming to file with the FDA first."

thumbnail.reasoning: All three candidates are legible at phone size with short, non-overlapping text and clear brand mark. #0 ("BUT MORE STOPPED") best matches the playbook's winning pattern: a reaction-style thumbnail with one labelled, emoting character (the surprised syringe) plus a concrete, honest twist (more people stopped treatment) that creates a genuine curiosity gap without overclaiming — exactly the kind of expectation-violation hook that past data shows performs best (reaction layouts median ~6.3% CTR vs weaker big-number/mystery layouts). #1 is solid but 'First Real Matchup' is a more generic tease that partially echoes 'First Results' already in the title, softening the curiosity gap. #2 relies purely on a question mark over a faceless syringe silhouette — no labelled character or visible emotion, which breaks the house rule and leans toward unproven 'mystery' framing that risks feeling vague/clickbaity relative to the other two, which pay off a specific, honest trade-off. #0 offers the strongest, most specific emotional pull while staying fully honest about the content (efficacy vs. dropout trade-off), making it the best choice among legible candidates.
